description: We’re 4 Electronics & Mechatronics Engineering students with hands-on experience designing, building and programming CubeSats and planning aerospace missions. We’re currently developing the OBC, EPS and COMMS systems for a satellite. Self-taught and driven by logic, hard engineering and passion. We see this hackathon as a chance to sharpen our front-end skills beyond hardware and firmware. If you bring commitment and an engineering mindset, you’ll fit right in!
summary:
CubeUp is a browser game where you design a CubeSat mission, from the contract to the first contact. A forest service needs sharp photos of wildfires in the Amazon. You have a 3U CubeSat, a mass limit, a budget and a launch date.
As in a real mission, each design decision affects the others. The orbit sets how much sunlight the panels get, how often the satellite passes over the ground station and how long it lives. A better camera produces more data, which needs a faster radio, which in turn needs more power, mass and money. When one subsystem changes, others have to be revised. Shared bars of money, time, mass, volume, power and data show the cost of every choice. Each room is a small simulation based on the real engineering calculation, and the game explains the reason behind each result. The first telemetry and photo from orbit show what the design achieved.
University CubeSat projects often outlast the students who build them, and much of their knowledge leaves when they graduate. In emerging space countries like Peru, it is also rarely taught. CubeUp lets a newcomer go through a complete mission and understand its trade-offs.
details:
The problem we saw
A CubeSat is small, but a university CubeSat program takes years, often longer than its students stay at the university. In INTISAT, a student CubeSat project we volunteered in, several generations graduated and left for industry before the satellite was finished, and much of what they had learned left with them. Link budgets, power budgets, attitude control and satellite operations are rarely part of the curriculum, so each new group had to start almost from zero. Peru's first aerospace engineering degree opened in 2025, at a single university. Other countries with emerging space programs face the same gap. Books and tools usually cover one subsystem at a time, so newcomers rarely see how the orbit, the power, the radio and the budget depend on each other.

What CubeUp does
The player joins a space agency and follows an 11-step mission path through 19 minigames. Each room is a part of the satellite:

  • Lobby: sign the contract, with its objective and its mass, volume and budget limits. At the Orbit Office, a short animated introduction explains the anatomy of an orbit and its parameters. The player then buys one of three popular orbits, or simulates a custom one and watches its eclipses, passes and lifetime change in real time. Each orbit comes with its price and launch date, and the launch date sets the time left to build.
  • Payload Lab: choose the camera. Design the attitude control, choosing sensors and actuators within the mission budget. Then fly a pass over the Amazon to check whether the pointing is good enough to frame the fires.
  • RF Lab: boot the flight computer and close the UHF link budget on a spectrum analyzer. Optional minigames cover the antenna balun, the antenna cut, the ground station antenna and the flight computer board design.
  • Power Lab: an end-of-life power budget that sizes the panels and the battery, then a 24-hour test of the operating modes.
  • Clean Room: check that everything fits in 3U and 4 kg, then assemble it in 3D. Optional minigames cover thermal blankets and a thermal vacuum test.
  • Launch and First Contact: the deployment from the rocket, then a problem real rideshare teams face. Radars track six objects on almost the same orbit, and the player finds theirs by matching the Doppler curve of its beacon. The first telemetry comes from the design: the battery charge, the temperature and whether the satellite has stopped tumbling. The first photo of the fire comes out sharp, shaky or cloudy depending on the design. The game ends with the CubeSat orbiting.

A final report gives up to three stars: the satellite fits in the deployer, stays within budget, and gets sharp photos down to the ground. It explains the causes, and the player can redesign and fly again.

How it works

  • Connected decisions. If the orbit changes, the attitude control and the power system must be redone. The camera produces megabytes per day, an onboard processor can reduce them, and the radio decides how many reach the ground. If the radio is too slow, the sharp photos never arrive. Several different designs can reach three stars.
  • Physical models. Orbits follow Kepler's laws plus the effect of Earth's flattening, which is what lets a sun-synchronous orbit cross the target at the same local time every day, and they include Earth's shadow. The link budget includes tropospheric and ionospheric losses. The power budget follows the CubeSat Handbook method, with load values from a real student CubeSat's preliminary budget.
  • Reviewable. All the physics lives in separate, automatically tested modules that a satellite engineer can read without knowing the game code.
  • Explanations. A mentor explains each concept with voice. The screen shows the effect of each decision instead of formulas, and when something fails the game explains what would happen in orbit.
  • Team play. Friends join the same agency with a four-letter room code, peer to peer and with no accounts, and can split the rooms the way a real team splits subsystems.
  • Runs anywhere. It opens from a link, needs no installation, and keeps working if the Wi-Fi drops.

Intended impact
CubeUp is meant as an onboarding tool for university CubeSat teams. A new volunteer can play the whole mission before working on the real satellite, which makes it easier to pass knowledge from one generation to the next. It also gives high school and first-year university students in countries without aerospace programs a first look at how a mission is engineered. It supports SDG 4 (quality education) and SDG 9 (industry and innovation), and its mission, wildfire monitoring, relates to SDGs 13 and 15.

NASA resources we used

  • Design and Develop Science Missions: the game follows its four segments. The user segment is the forest service, whose need sets the requirements. The space segment is the subsystem rooms. The launch segment is the Orbit Office, where buying an orbit includes the ride. The ground segment is the Lima station, the link budget and First Contact.
  • CubeSat 101: the mission phases from concept to operations behind the game's path, and operational rules shown in the game, such as waiting 30 minutes after release before deploying panels and antennas.
  • NASA Blue Marble and Blue Marble Next Generation: the Earth on every globe, with a high-resolution image of the Andes and the Amazon.

Tools and technologies

  • TypeScript and JavaScript.
  • Babylon.js for the 3D rooms, globes and cinematics.
  • HTML, CSS and SVG for the simulation consoles.
  • Vite.
  • The Node.js test runner for the physics.
  • PeerJS for online rooms.
  • Firebase Hosting.
  • Google Cloud Text-to-Speech for the mentor's voice.

What makes it creative
Each engineering step is a room in the agency, and each minigame uses the same calculation an engineer would do. The first photo and the first telemetry at the end are produced by the player's own design. The game also shows how teams identify their satellite after a rideshare launch using the Doppler shift of its beacon, a step that educational games rarely include.

Next steps

  • Validate orbits and lifetimes against GMAT.
  • Add contracts for other CubeSat sizes.
  • Share the mission state and roles in team mode.
  • Release a Spanish version for Latin America.
  • Test it as onboarding with university CubeSat teams in Peru.
